claim_scope: Project 2025 Medicaid financing proposals and the Georgetown analysis’s projected risks only. Do not claim SNAP block-grant conversion, enactment, implementation, or realized recipient/state harms.

proposal.title: Project 2025 Proposed Medicaid Funding Caps
proposal.description_short: Georgetown says Project 2025 proposed Medicaid block grants or per-capita caps; the analysis discusses projected risks, not implemented changes.
proposal.description_medium: Georgetown’s Center for Children and Families says Project 2025 proposed replacing federal-state Medicaid matching with block grants or per-capita caps. The center notes that the blueprint does not explain how caps would be set or adjusted and warns they could fail to keep pace with enrollment or health costs. The analysis describes a proposal and projected risks, not enacted changes or SNAP implementation.
proposal.description_long: The Center for Children and Families at Georgetown reviewed Medicaid provisions in Project 2025 and described a proposal to replace the federal-state matching arrangement with federal funding caps structured as block grants or per-capita caps. Under the current arrangement, federal contributions track a fixed percentage of state Medicaid costs; under the proposed caps described by the center, federal payments would instead be limited to an aggregate amount or a per-beneficiary amount, irrespective of states’ actual costs. The article says the blueprint does not specify how caps would initially be set or adjusted. It warns that caps that fail to keep pace with enrollment or health-care costs could reduce federal spending over time and leave states facing more costs, including during recessions, natural disasters, or public-health emergencies. Those are the center’s projections about a policy proposal. The article does not document that Medicaid financing was converted, that SNAP was block-granted, or that states or recipients experienced those projected outcomes. It also does not establish an enacted law or implementation date. This account is limited to the Medicaid proposal described in the Georgetown analysis.

source_to_fact_mapping.supports: Georgetown CCF describes Project 2025 as proposing conversion of federal Medicaid funding to block grants or per-capita caps; it notes the plan’s unspecified cap-setting details and analyzes possible cost-growth effects.
source_to_fact_mapping.limits: Policy analysis and projected risk only; no enactment or observed effects. This source does not establish Project 2025 SNAP block-grant terms.

claim_scope: The April 29, 2019 Senate message and the July 2019 UN depositary communication. Describe the Senate return request and non-party intent; do not say the U.S. withdrew from a ratified treaty or that the April message erased its signature.

proposal.title: Trump Asked the Senate to Return the Arms Trade Treaty
proposal.description_short: In April 2019, Trump asked the Senate to return the Arms Trade Treaty; the United States had signed but not ratified it.
proposal.description_medium: In an April 29, 2019 message, President Donald Trump said the United States did not intend to become a party to the Arms Trade Treaty and asked the Senate to return it. The country had signed the treaty in 2013 but had not ratified it. A July communication to the UN depositary said the United States had no legal obligations arising from its signature.
proposal.description_long: On April 29, 2019, President Donald Trump sent the Senate a message about the Arms Trade Treaty. He said he had concluded that it was not in the United States’ interest to become a party and requested that the Senate return the treaty to him. That is the action stated in the archived message: return from Senate consideration, not withdrawal from a treaty the United States had ratified. The United States had signed the treaty on September 25, 2013, but had not ratified it. In a communication received by the UN depositary on July 18, 2019, the United States said it did not intend to become a party and had no legal obligations arising from its signature. The official records support describing the Senate request and the later statement of non-party intent. They do not support saying the United States left a binding treaty or that the April message itself erased the signature. This account omits the reported April 26 NRA convention announcement because these two primary records establish the April 29 message and July communication, not the convention event.

source_to_fact_mapping.supports: The April 29, 2019 message says it was not in U.S. interest to become a party and requests that the treaty be withdrawn from the Senate and returned.
source_to_fact_mapping.limits: Does not say the U.S. withdrew its signature or left a treaty it had ratified.

source_to_fact_mapping.limits: The later notice does not change the text of the April 29 Senate message or establish the April 26 NRA-event report.

proposal.title: EO 13780 Specified 2017 Entry and Refugee Pauses
proposal.description_short: Executive Order 13780 provided for a 90-day entry suspension for nationals of six countries and a separate 120-day refugee pause, subject to exceptions.
proposal.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017. Its text provided for a 90-day suspension of entry for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to exceptions, and a separate 120-day pause in refugee admissions. The order specified March 16, 2017, as its effective time. This describes the order’s stated terms, not proof of implementation or later court action.
proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017. The order’s text provided for a 90-day suspension of entry for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen, subject to stated exceptions. The provision applied to people outside the United States on the effective date who lacked a valid visa at the order’s specified January 27 cutoff and still lacked one on the effective date. The order separately provided for a 120-day pause in refugee admissions, also subject to exceptions, and specified an effective time of March 16, 2017. Its six-country entry list did not include Iraq, which had appeared in the January order. These are the terms and schedule printed in the Federal Register. The order text alone does not establish whether or how each restriction took effect in practice, explain later court injunctions, or show the outcome of subsequent litigation. The earlier Associated Press citation concerned an unrelated fact-check and is not used as support here.
